highlights: Volcanic Kona Coast sanctuary where thatched hale, ocean rituals and Hawaiian heritage glow
description:
Kona Village, a Rosewood Resort sits on the lava-edged Kona Coast of Hawai‘i Island, spread across 81 acres at Kahuwai Bay within the storied ahupua‘a of Kaʻūpūlehu. The setting is deeply tied to place: a fishing village long before it became a beloved 1960s resort, then a dormant shoreline after the 2011 tsunami, now carefully revived as a low-slung Hawaiian retreat. Its return has been framed around cultural consultation and a lighter environmental footprint, rather than a simple reconstruction of the past.

The resort’s 150 hale and kauhale are raised lightly above the landscape, with thatched roofs, oversized lanais and many outdoor showers. Interiors by NICOLEHOLLIS and architecture by Walker Warner draw on local craft, coconut-husk textures, basalt rock and softened tropical modernism rather than nostalgia. Thirty-seven kauhale suites add deeper privacy, with selected oceanfront and garden residences offering pools, hot tubs and butler service.

Dining keeps close to the land and sea. Moana anchors the village with Pacific Rim cooking informed by Hawai‘i Island ingredients, while Kahuwai Cookhouse & Market draws on paniolo ranch culture and kiawe-fired flavours. Talk Story Bar and the restored Shipwreck Bar bring back two of the original resort’s social rituals; produce from the on-site Kahiko Mālaʻai garden threads through the menus.

Days move between Asaya Spa, four outdoor pools, a fitness centre, tennis and pickleball courts, complimentary bicycles, sailing, snorkeling and canoe paddles on Kahuwai Bay. A cultural centre shares the history of the land, while the resort’s solar microgrid, zero-waste commitment and LEED Gold spaces give its rebirth a quietly progressive edge.

highlights: Polished Cable Beach enclave with Bahamian elegance, private sands and Café Boulud
description:
Rosewood Baha Mar occupies a polished enclave on Nassau’s Cable Beach, where 3,000 feet of white sand places the resort within the wider Baha Mar world while keeping its own calmer, residential mood. Downtown Nassau, the National Art Gallery of The Bahamas and the Queen’s Staircase are a short drive away, with Ardastra Gardens, Nassau Botanical Gardens and New Providence’s marinas extending the island context beyond the beach.

The resort’s 221 guestrooms, suites and villas are styled as a contemporary Bahamian estate, using coral, blue and lavender tones that echo sea, sky and sunset. Rooms open to private balconies and outdoor living areas, while the three- and six-bedroom villas add greater seclusion, residential space and plunge pools. Glass amenity vessels and broader plastic-reduction measures add a practical sustainability note to the island glamour.

Café Boulud The Bahamas brings Daniel Boulud’s French repertoire to a beachside setting, joined by Costa for Latin-accented coastal cooking, Manor Bar for classic cocktails, The Library for afternoon tea and Champagne, Tingum on the Sand for barefoot dining, and a bright Breakfast Café. It is a culinary programme designed for lingering rather than resort haste.

Facilities are extensive: Sense, A Rosewood Spa and salon, pools and luxury cabanas, exclusive beach access, non-motorized watersports, a state-of-the-art fitness centre, Rosewood Explorers for children, tennis, luxury shopping and the Jack Nicklaus-designed Royal Blue golf course. The result is a refined Nassau resort with both private-villa ease and the scale of a larger destination playground.

highlights: Gardened Silicon Valley retreat where Santa Cruz Mountain views soften contemporary polish
description:
Rosewood Sand Hill sits on 16 gardened acres in Menlo Park, one mile west of Stanford University and directly on Silicon Valley’s most influential stretch of Sand Hill Road. Venture-capital offices may be close by, yet the hotel looks more toward flowering courtyards, open terraces and the Santa Cruz Mountains than toward corporate polish. Its low profile gives meetings, weekends and longer stays a resort calm rarely found in the Stanford–Palo Alto corridor.

The 121 rooms and suites interpret relaxed California ranch architecture with a quietly residential tone: vaulted ceilings in some upper-floor rooms, marble baths, original art, substantial technology and private balconies or terraces that draw the landscape inward. Larger suites and the two-bedroom Presidential Villa extend the indoor-outdoor idea with fireplaces, generous parlours, private lawns and mountain-facing glass.

Madera is the social and culinary heart of the hotel, serving Northern California cooking shaped by local, seasonal and sustainably sourced ingredients, with the dining room and terrace angled toward the hills. Madera Bar brings the same view to cocktails and light dishes, while Bici Coffee gives the property a casual daytime rhythm. Private dining is set within Madera for smaller gatherings.

The resort-like amenities are unusually complete for the Stanford–Palo Alto corridor. Asaya Spa includes 13 treatment rooms, a movement studio and a holistic wellness programme; elsewhere are an outdoor pool, fitness room, cycling experiences and guided outdoor adventures. From here, Palo Alto, Stanford’s galleries and gardens, Woodside trails, coastal redwood drives and the wineries of the Santa Cruz Mountains frame the hotel as both Silicon Valley base and Northern California retreat.

highlights: Canalside Georgetown intimacy with Wolfgang Puck dining and capital skyline views
description:
Rosewood Washington, D.C. rests beside the historic C&O Canal in Georgetown, giving the capital a smaller, more residential expression of luxury than its grand avenue hotels. The setting places canal paths, townhouse-lined streets, boutiques and the Georgetown waterfront immediately around the property, with the Potomac, Kennedy Center, museums and monuments reached easily across the city. Nearby M Street and Wisconsin Avenue add Georgetown’s retail energy, while the towpath keeps the immediate mood quietly historic.

The 55-room property has the air of a private address, especially in its adjacent historic townhouses, which extend the hotel into the neighbourhood. Rooms and suites are composed in a refined contemporary style with warm woods, tailored upholstery and generous light; signature suites such as the Rosewood Suite and Presidential Suite add larger living areas, fireplaces or memorable Georgetown views. Its compact scale is central to the atmosphere, keeping arrivals, dining and wellness deliberately personal.

Dining is shaped by Wolfgang Puck. CUT D.C. brings the chef’s steakhouse language to Washington with beef, seafood and vegetable-led cooking informed by Mid-Atlantic farms and fisheries, while CUT Bar and Lounge adds a club-like space for cocktails and live music. CUT Above rises to the roof for skyline views and seasonal drinks, and afternoon tea softens the tempo during the day.

Wellness is intimate rather than sprawling: in-room spa services, a rooftop fitness centre, and a rooftop pool with a built-in fireplace and views across the city. Private gatherings use CUT Above and other compact event spaces, while curated Potomac River cruises connect the hotel’s canalside character to wider Washington. The mood is discreet, polished and distinctly Georgetown.

highlights: Roaring Twenties Vancouver landmark with Art Deco glamour and Hawksworth dining
description:
Rosewood Hotel Georgia stands at Georgia and Howe Streets in downtown Vancouver, a 1927 landmark restored with the confidence of a grand city hotel and the restraint of a contemporary residence. The address places Robson Street shopping, galleries, theatres and the Vancouver Art Gallery close by, while Stanley Park, the seawall, Granville Island, Yaletown and the North Shore Mountains give the city its rare urban-outdoor range. Its restored public spaces preserve a ceremonial sense of arrival without turning the hotel into a museum.

The hotel’s 156 rooms and suites layer light blues, ivory and chocolate tones against the building’s historic frame, with softly residential furnishings and spa-inspired bathrooms. Its premier Lord Stanley and Rosewood suites add two bedrooms, private rooftop terraces, plunge pools and gardens, with the Rosewood Suite able to connect for a larger three-bedroom arrangement.

Dining is a major part of the hotel’s identity. Hawksworth Restaurant, from chef David Hawksworth, brings polished contemporary Canadian cooking to an elegant room off the lobby, joined by 1927 Lounge for afternoon tea, The Georgia Bar for live entertainment and cocktails, Reflections The Garden Terrace for open-air dining, Prophecy for late-evening conversation and Bel Café for pastries and coffee.

The wellness offering includes Sense, A Rosewood Spa, a fitness centre and a 52-foot indoor saltwater lap pool. Private dining and event spaces keep the hotel active for Vancouver occasions, while curated experiences range from FlyOver Canada and Stanley Park to whale-watching trips. Its appeal comes from the balance of Roaring Twenties architecture, restored craftsmanship and immediate access to one of North America’s most naturally dramatic cities.
